sections.figure_alt: A feedback path and a feedforward path add to form the plant command.
sections.body_md:
Feedback acts only after an error exists. Feedforward acts on a signal that is already known: the reference, or a measured disturbance. The two paths add at the plant command. Because the feedforward path is outside the loop, it does not change the loop gain, the sensitivity function, or the stability margins. It changes the particular response to the signal it measures.

That split is what a two-degree-of-freedom controller is for. One degree of freedom sets how hard the loop fights uncertainty and unmeasured disturbances. The other sets how the known reference or the known load shows up in the output. A good feedback design can then stay put while the feedforward path is adjusted.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
If a disturbance \(d\) adds at the plant input, the cancelling command is \(u = -d\). If \(d\) adds at the output of a plant with DC gain \(P\), the steady command that cancels it is \(u = -d/P\).

A reference prefilter \(F\) in front of a unity-feedback loop produces the overall map \(F\, T\), with \(T = L/(1+L)\). The DC choice \(F = 1/T(0)\) makes a constant reference come through with gain 1. Open-loop inversion of a model \(P_0\) uses \(F = 1/P_0\). On the true plant the gain is \(P/P_0\), which equals 1 only when the model matches.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A heater has DC gain 3.5 from valve command to temperature. A measured inlet disturbance of 0.8 adds at the valve, so the cancelling feedforward command is \(-0.8\). Separately, the static inverse that would turn a reference step into the same steady temperature with no feedback is \(1/3.5 \approx 0.286\). If the real gain is a little higher than 3.5, that inverse overshoots, and the feedback loop, if it is present, only has to trim the residual.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The sign has to oppose the disturbance. A flipped sign doubles the load instead of removing it. Input and output disturbances use different formulas: dividing by \(P\) is correct only when the disturbance is downstream of the plant. A prefilter cannot supply the infinite DC gain of an integrator, so it does not by itself remove the steady error of a type-0 loop. Inverting a right-half-plane zero builds an unstable filter. Invert the stable, well-known part of the model and leave the rest to feedback.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The same two paths reappear when state feedback is combined with a reference model and an observer. The feedback piece stabilizes and rejects what was not measured. The feedforward piece carries the planned trajectory. Saturation still has to be respected, because a perfect inverse can ask for a command the actuator cannot produce.
